newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Opposition says Mandela speech lacks substance.
newsitem.headline: Opposition says Mandela speech lacks substance.

text.p: South African opposition parties said they were disappointed with President Nelson Mandela's opening address to parliament on Friday, charging it lacked substance on how implement agreed goals.

"With regard to some of the fundamental issues we have already lost too much time. We want to see implemented what the president said," said F. W. de Klerk, South Africa's last apartheid president and now leader of the National Party (NP).
He said the NP applauded Mandela's stated goals, which included a better life for the poor, but felt he had spelled out too little about how they should be achieved.

"The failures of the ANC (African National Congress) government were whitewashed. It is not good enough to admit failure, one must address the failures and that has not been sufficiently done to my mind," de Klerk said.

Tony Leon, leader of the liberal Democratic Party, said investors would be disappointed in the lack of substance about how to implement the seven-month-old macro-economic strategy for growth, employment and redistribution, known as GEAR.

"On the economic side, we heard nothing today except a restatement of the principles of GEAR. What everyone was crying out for was some radical, bold move to actually drive it forward, but there is nothing new," he said.

Markets reacted favourably to Mandela's renewed commitment to the phased removal of remaining foreign exchange controls, to the privatisation of state enterprises and to implementation of the macro-economic strategy unveiled last June.
The rand, which lost almost 30 percent of its value against the dollar last year, strengthened to a seven-month high after Mandela's address.
Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, leader of the Inkatha Freedom Party and Mandela's strongest black rival, said the speech outlined laudable goals but was unconvincing.
"The ideas were good, but there was not enough content. Only if what he says we are going to do does in fact take off, then I think we can have hope," he said.

ANC cabinet minister Kader Asmal said Mandela had given a sober mid-term assessment of the country's achievements, failures and challenges half way through the first five-year term of democratic government.
"There was some interesting self-criticism, which I think is necessary, but it is not opportunistic. It is a sober revue of where we are," he said.
Constand Viljoen, leader of the white-separatist Freedom Front, said Mandela underplayed the country's crime crisis.
"We think the President is a bit wishy washy on the idea of law and order. What he said was not really convincing," he said.
Mandela said the government would renew the fight against soaring crime and promised to crack down on corruption within the police force and amongst border-control staff.
